/-!
# Additive complements

Two sets of naturals are *additive complements* when their sumset contains every large integer.
-/

open Filter

open scoped Pointwise

/-- `A` and `B` are *additive complements* if `A + B` contains all large integers. -/
def IsAdditiveComplement (A B : Set ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, n ∈ A + B

theorem IsAdditiveComplement.symm {A B : Set ℕ} (h : IsAdditiveComplement A B) :
    IsAdditiveComplement B A := by
  filter_upwards [h] with n hn using by rwa [Set.addCommMonoid.add_comm]

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/785.lean:79–81, `IsAdditiveComplement` correctly allows zero as a summand, but `counting` excludes it. No hypothesis excludes zero from A or B. This changes the excess, not merely finitely many values. There are admissible infinite exact pairs for which the asserted divergence fails: take Ruzsa's positive sets C,D from §3, choose his freely growing parameters so u_{k+1}/(p_k u_k) → ∞, and put A = {c-1 : c ∈ C}, B = D. Complementarity is preserved, and the positive-only product ratio still tends to 1. At x_k = u_{k+1}-1, however, the Lean excess equals C(x_k)D(x_k)-x_k-D(x_k) ≤ O(u_k) - (x_k-r)/p_k → -∞. Thus the theorem is false for sets admitted by its hypotheses.
findings.source_evidence: Chen–Fang, On a conjecture of Sárközy and Szemerédi, Acta Arith. 169 (2015), p.47, explicitly uses nonnegative sets with T(x)=|T∩[0,x]| when stating the divergence theorem (https://www.impan.pl/shop/en/publication/transaction/download/product/82737). Ruzsa, Exact additive complements, §1, instead explicitly assumes positive integers; §3 supplies the construction and estimates above (https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.00812). The Erdős page uses counts over [1,x], consistent with the positive-integer convention.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the reusable library predicate unchanged. With the current counting function, require `0 ∉ A` and `0 ∉ B`, for example in the problem-local exact-complement predicate. Alternatively, consistently adopt the nonnegative convention `counting A x := (A ∩ Set.Iic x).ncard` and update the documentation.

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/785.lean:108–111, the symmetric `IsExactAdditiveComplement A B` hypothesis does not designate A as the thinner set, yet the conclusion forbids an O(A(x)^c) bound for either possible ordering of A,B. This is false even for strictly positive sets. Infinite exact complements exist, and Narkiewicz's dichotomy lets their larger member be labelled A with x ≤ A(x)^2 eventually. Exactness gives |A(x)B(x)-x| ≤ x eventually, hence the very O(A(x)^2) bound this declaration excludes at c=2. The latter implication was proved in the scratch Lean file.
findings.source_evidence: Chen–Fang (2015), Theorem 0.2, states an eventual lower bound by `min{A(x),B(x)}^M` for every M>1, not by a power of an arbitrarily labelled member (https://www.impan.pl/shop/en/publication/transaction/download/product/82737). Ruzsa §1 explicitly says, before presenting the O(A(x)^c) corollary, 'For the sequel we will assume ... A is small and B is large.' His Theorem 1.1 gives the growth dichotomy (https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.00812). The abbreviated Erdős webpage omits this qualification.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the Big-O comparison function by `(fun x => (min (counting A x) (counting B x) : ℝ) ^ c)`. Alternatively, add the hypothesis `Tendsto (fun x => (counting A (2*x) : ℝ) / (counting A x : ℝ)) atTop (𝓝 1)` selecting the smaller member. Use a consistent counting/domain convention as well.

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/785.lean:145–152, the complement hypothesis admits zero, while the excess counts only positive elements. The translated Ruzsa construction described for `Erdos785.erdos_785` satisfies both infinitude hypotheses and `IsExactAdditiveComplement`, but its Lean excess tends to -∞ along an unbounded subsequence. At ε=1/2, the left side of either proposed lower bound is nonnegative, so neither branch can hold eventually. Allowing a swap of A and B does not repair this counting mismatch.
findings.source_evidence: Ruzsa, Exact additive complements, Theorem 1.2 explicitly concerns infinite sets of positive integers and bounds their full counting-function excess by `(1-o(1)) a*(x)/A(x)`; §3 provides the counterexample after translation when zero is allowed but omitted from counting (https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.00812).
findings.suggested_fix: Require `0 ∉ A` and `0 ∉ B` in the exact-complement hypotheses while retaining counts over [1,x], or consistently count all nonnegative elements. The disjunction encoding the possible swap can remain unchanged.

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/785.lean:162–166, `IsAdditiveComplement A B` permits zero, but the conclusion uses the positive-only counting function without positivity restrictions on the sets. The translated infinite exact pair from Ruzsa's construction has ratio limit, hence EReal limsup, equal to 1 < 3-sqrt(3), so it satisfies every hypothesis. Its Lean excess is nevertheless unbounded below along a subsequence, contradicting the conclusion. Fixing only the local exact-complement predicate would not fix this direct use of the library predicate.
findings.source_evidence: Fang–Chen, On additive complements (2010), §1 defines nonnegative complements and counts every a≤x, including zero (https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/2010-138-06/S0002-9939-10-10205-6/S0002-9939-10-10205-6.pdf). Chen's 2016 Graz slides, Theorem 5 on p.13, state the improved threshold 3-sqrt(3) with that nonnegative convention (https://static.uni-graz.at/fileadmin/veranstaltungen/additive2016/Talks/chen_yg_slides.pdf).
findings.suggested_fix: Add `0 ∉ A` and `0 ∉ B` to this theorem, or change the problem's counting function consistently to include zero. Do not change the reusable complement predicate merely to accommodate this use site.

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/785.lean:173–177, the question ranges over nonnegative sets whose sums may use zero, but tests divergence of an excess that omits zero from both counts. The translated Ruzsa pair has limsup 1 < 3/2 and fails the proposed divergence. Consequently the right-hand proposition is false under the present definitions for a reason absent from Chen's conjecture. This is not a disproof or status update of the cited conjecture.
findings.source_evidence: Chen's Graz 2016 slides define additive complements of nonnegative integers on p.5 and pose this exact 3/2-threshold conjecture on p.17 (https://static.uni-graz.at/fileadmin/veranstaltungen/additive2016/Talks/chen_yg_slides.pdf). The accompanying Chen–Fang paper explicitly defines the relevant count as |T∩[0,x]| on p.47. Ruzsa §1's alternative convention uses positive sets throughout (https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.00812).
findings.suggested_fix: Inside the universally quantified question, require `0 ∉ A` and `0 ∉ B`, or consistently use counts over [0,x]. Retain the open status and unknown answer for the corrected conjecture.

reformulations.difference: Uses eventual membership in the pointwise sumset along `atTop : Filter ℕ`, rather than explicitly saying that the sumset has finite complement or giving a threshold and summand witnesses.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Mathlib's Set.mem_add gives n∈A+B iff ∃a∈A, ∃b∈B, a+b=n. Filter.eventually_atTop gives ∃N, ∀n≥N, that property. Nat.cofinite_eq_atTop also identifies the definition with `(A+B)ᶜ.Finite`. Both equivalences were proved in scratch. Empty sets fail, two finite sets fail, and a singleton can legitimately complement an appropriate infinite set.

reformulations.difference: Its infinite exact-complement existence statement uses positive-only counts, whereas Chen's presentation of Danzer's theorem counts all nonnegative elements.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Both sets are explicitly infinite. Write a₀(x)=a₊(x)+εA and b₀(x)=b₊(x)+εB, where εA,εB∈{0,1} indicate membership of zero. Since a₊ and b₊ tend to infinity, a₀b₀/(a₊b₊)→1. Thus the exactness limit is equivalent under the two counting conventions for the same infinite complementary pair. This equivalence concerns the leading ratio only; it does not justify using the positive-only excess in the findings above.
